utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see Mr. Van de Vliet is on the witness stand. Do you have some answers for us, Mr. Van de Vliet? MR. VAN DE VLIET: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just say to you, Mr. Van de Vliet, that the memo that you wrote, I hope everybody has got a copy of it. We have read and we understand what you explained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry but we are not in possession of this memo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not in possession of the memo? In that event, then you better go through it. You might as well go through it, Mr. Van de Vliet. MR. VAN DE VLIET: Yes, Your Honour, maybe it's just wise if I just lead you through it. Maybe I shouldn't focus on every single detail but just present the overall picture. As I promised I would go back to my staff and find out the details of the planning of the resource arrangement for this Defence team. We have to go through a little procedure before we finally make the decision and that involves obtaining an official submission by the Defence team on the complexity level, a consultation process with the Chamber on both the complexity level presented by the Defence and the duration of the trial, and then we make a determination. The final submission by the Defence was made on the 11th of December. We have had the consultation with Chamber representatives on the 13th; on the 14th the decision was made, 14th of December 2005, on the allocation of resources for trial. We insisted then as we always do and we need for our finance department to follow-up on an invoice in which the lead counsel will present how the resources have to be allocated over the team, the Defence team, and we have not obtained such an invoice before the 5th of January, and after the 5th of January we have processed that invoice in accordance with our usual regulations. And after yesterday's -- maybe it is good to reassure you that after yesterday's hearing I have verified with the finance department that the payment will be made this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's meant by this week? Can a date not be given? MR. VAN DE VLIET: I guess that means by the end of this week it will be made. Before the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the Chamber is completely unsatisfied by this arrangement, Mr. Van de Vliet. In your memo you said that on the 14th of December a letter from OLAD to the Defence team regarding the complexity level and allocation of resources was requested, was -- and including a request for a pro forma. Today you're telling us that on that date, the 14th of December, a determination was made, a decision was made on the allocation of resources for trial. Now, if a decision was made on the 14th of December on the allocation of resources, I cannot understand why, at this stage, that payment has not yet been made. And then we've been told that payment will be made sometime this week. MR. VAN DE VLIET: Your Honour, we cannot make a payment without an invoice. There is the way the system works. And the invoice was not submitted to us before the 5th of January so after the 5th of January, we received the invoice, we have processed it in accordance with our usual procedures and then it goes to the finance department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How long does it take to process an invoice? MR. VAN DE VLIET: For my office, we service 17 Defence teams. For your information, it will take two weeks. And then it will go to the finance department, which will use -- we -- on average for the Tribunal, to process an invoice of the Defence we will take a month. Two weeks my office, two weeks the other departments that are involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Van de Vliet, what steps are in place for expedition in circumstances such as this one. And what steps have you taken to implement them? MR. VAN DE VLIET: Could you be more specific, Your Honour? I'm just wondering whether you're referring to the procedure, the determination procedure on the complexity level and the duration of a case for processing an invoice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I mean what steps exist for expediting the fact of the payment itself and the delivery of the 10 per cent to the Defence, both as a general rule and what steps have you taken in this particular case for expedition. MR. VAN DE VLIET: Yes. Generally, the invoices of Defence teams, and there are quite a number of them in this Tribunal, go through a number of different offices within the Registry and the UN administration. First office where it comes is my office, the office of legal aid and detention matters. Within this office we look at the invoice, we check the amounts and we sign off on it. Then it will go to the administration and it will see, I think, two or three offices within that building as well. And then it will be paid. In this case, like I said we received the invoice on the 5th of January. In spite of having made the decision on the 14th of December, as of the 5th of January we have processed the invoice. It has reached the finance department. I have verified yesterday and asked whether the invoice had been processed. It had not been but it was in their possession, and I have asked for them to expedite this invoice ASAP and they assured me it would be done before the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Van de Vliet. Mr. Milovancevic, I hope you now hear the explanation given. Mr. Van de Vliet says that the pro forma invoice, without which no payment can be made, was only delivered to them by yourselves on the 5th of January. It takes two weeks for his office to process the document. It takes another two weeks for the finance department to process the document. It's a whole month so that at the earliest you would expect to get payment by the 4th of February. However, he has tried to expedite the payment and the promise is that the Defence team will be given some -- the payment by the end of this week. Unless you dispute having submitted the document -- the pro forma account on the 5th of January, it doesn't seem as if much can be done about this matter to expedite the payment any faster than we are now being told. Do you have any comments to make? Please be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. It's correct that the pro forma arrived on that date. Just a brief bit of info in addition. We were also asked to address the question of the assessment of the complexity level of the entire trial. Therefore, what we sent was not a mere pro forma. There was a serious job to be done, in a manner of speaking. Therefore we sent a letter on the 5th of January asking for the Registry's understanding. The trial was due to begin on the 16th and we were running out of time. That's all we asked for and that's all I have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. But I hope you do understand, then, that with that pro forma invoice having been submitted on the 5th of January only, it doesn't look like the Defence is without blame on the matter. I don't want to take the matter much further than that. I would imagine that, as Mr. Van de Vliet promises us, payment will be made this week sometime, and that the Defence will be put in a position to prepare for their case. Mr. Van de Vliet, thank you very much. You may be excused from court. MR. VAN DE VLIET: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just had one small housekeeping matter to take care of and I thought I could do it before the witness is brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You please do so. We also have some housekeeping matters. You go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. This is with regard to the translation of the map, Exhibit, which I believe is Exhibit 3. Yeah, I'm getting a nod from the Registry so it's Exhibit 3, and we have a translation which I'll hand up now. I propose, if it's possible, to just add the translation and the way the translation is referenced to the exhibit, if that's possible. Or maybe it will have to be given a separate exhibit. With the assistance of the usher if we could hand it to the Chamber and to the parties. I just want to take one quick, brief moment to explain it. It's pretty self-evident but it's a little odd because it's a map and there is text all over the map, I just want to make sure that it's clear how we've indicated the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe then we should ask that it be given an exhibit number. Can we give it an exhibit number that ties it to the original map? Thank you very much. Can I suggest, Mr. Whiting, that actually this has to do -- unlike housekeeping, it's more to do with the trial itself, the evidence itself. Can we do it last?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's deal with -- first with the actual housekeeping that the Bench has to raise. There has been an approach by the Registry to say that on Friday, the 20th, I suppose, we are supposed to be sitting in Courtroom II on that day from quarter past two. Due to the refurbishments that are taking place and other little logistical problems that have arisen, a request is being made that our session, the session of this Chamber on that day starts at 8.00 in the morning and ends an hour earlier than the normal session. That would be because we will not have started at 9, we will have started at 8. We would then end at quarter to one or quarter past one -- quarter to one instead of quarter to two. The Bench has conditionally agreed, pending whether this is convenient for all the parties, to share the matter at 8.00 on that day, and can -- if the parties are in a position to give an indication now whether they would be able to sit at that time, the Bench would appreciate that, but if not, maybe tomorrow you can give an indication. Let's start with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We are available, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're available. Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are available too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much and the Bench is most obliged to both parties for being available at such short notice. Very well, then. Then in case the -- in case tomorrow it is not mentioned specifically that we are adjourning to Courtroom II at 8.00, we will make a note of that, that it is Courtroom II at 8.00 on Friday morning. The other issue that arose -- and this really came up as a consideration for all the parties that are involved in the case, in particular the interpreters, thus far, or let me take a step back and say, the Bench had been advised that the tapes go for one and a half hours, that there is a need for a 30-minute break after every one and a half hours for corrections to be made and for the delayed broadcast, and we've been trying to stick to that since we began. A suggestion has been put to the Bench that one and a half hours might perhaps be a little too long, particularly for the interpreters, who I'm told need greater concentration than anyone of us in doing their work, and that maybe if we made one hour 15 minute sessions, that would be to their benefit. If we do it that way, it looks to me like we would then have three equal sessions of one hour 15 minutes. As things stand now we've been having two, one and a half hour sessions and a 45 minute session at the end. There are pros and cons on both sides. The pro what we have been doing is that the last session before we knock off and everybody else is tired is that it's shorter; it's 45 minutes. The con for that is that the interpreters are being kept for one and a half hours and this is tiring on them. The other one, all hours will be one hour -- all sessions will be one hour 15 minutes, so the last session is equal to all the other sessions, no shorter thing. That's the con. The pro is that all of them are shorter for the interpreters. What is convenient for the parties? Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think we would have a slight preference for the alternative suggestion, that is the equal segments during the day but we are in the hands of the Chamber. We will do whatever the Chamber deems best. But I do think for the benefit of the interpreters, and also the witness because the witness is also often under a lot of strain and needs breaks, I think the one hour 15 minutes could be beneficial. And let me just add that, of course, we always try to keep track of the time and when the Court desires to break but if we miss that, the Court, of course, will let us know if it's the -- the time has come to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, sure. Mr. Milovancevic, which segment do you prefer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we believe that the solution you're talking about, with one hour 15 minute sessions with half hour breaks is perfectly all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, obviously, we have made this change, I'm talking about interpreters whose input we haven't heard. Maybe in fairness, let's just hear. Mr. Interpreter, would you perhaps make any input?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are entirely in your hands, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The arrangement is being made in consideration of your -- of you. We would appreciate it if you can indicate your preference.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This would require a consultation with the remaining two booths and perhaps I can give you some feedback during the next break if that's okay. Thank you, Your Honours. I'm not in a position to do so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Pending your input, we will go on three equal sessions pending the input from the interpreters later. Okay? So today we will go one hour 15 minutes at a time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those were the housekeeping issues that I wanted to raise at this time. The Bench wanted to raise at this time. Mr. Whiting, you wanted to explain the map before Mr. Milovancevic continues with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just briefly because I think it is pretty self explanatory, but the way the document was translated it was somehow translated by different pages so the references is to page -- first page, second page, because the translation unit obviously got it in a different form than the map as we see it. However, what I have done is -- with the assistance of an interpreter is to match up the passages with the assistance of an interpreter is to match up the passages with the places on the map with the numbering system and that's it. So it's clear what is -- what refers to what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic, before we call you, may the witness please come in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness, may the Court officers please give us an exhibit number to the map and the interpretation? To this map, which is now numbered, and the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that would be Exhibits 15 and 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now which is 15, the map itself? And the interpretation 16?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Exhibit number 15 is the map and Exhibit number 16 is the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, Mr. Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you are reminded once again that you are still bound by the declaration you took at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness is yours, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, yesterday when we broke off, we were discussing the meeting that the Serbian delegation had in Belgrade in November of 1990, the meeting with Mr. Jovic and Mr. Milosevic. Can you tell us, Mr. Ante Markovic, the then Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, was he present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any explanation for his absence?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that he was not going to see us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. This was in late 1990 and let us go back to mid-1990. Mr. Dzakula you mentioned the first multi-party elections. You said that you voted for the party of democratic changes led by Mr. Racan. What happened following the first multi-party elections, both in terms of what happened to you and to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The new authorities were set up, the new government came to power, led by Croatian Democratic Union, and they started restructuring the state adopted new laws, regulations, new names, coats of arms, emblems, flags, and so on. Therefore everything started changing, changing considerably in relation to how things were. These changes came as a surprise to the Serbs. They did not expect things to take this course especially these changes related to new symbols, coat of arms, flag, name and so on. Later on, they started preparing and then adopted a new constitution that had a number of new provisions. All of this caused concern among the Serbs. They expected other changes to occur, not these changes, which were surprising to them. Steps were made to prepare secession from Yugoslavia. On a daily basis, there was more and more talk against Yugoslavia. It was said that there were way too many Serbs in the judiciary, police, military, and so on, and that it ought to be changed. And in that sense, people were being dismissed from the television station, big companies, the judiciary and so on. The policemen were sent into early retirement. That option was offered to them in order to employ new officers. As I have told you the symbols were changed as well. Instead of a five-pointed star, a new symbol was adopted, chequerboard flag. The first proposal was to have this chequerboard designed with red and white, and later on, they opted for red colour because that was the symbol used, the independent state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. Was that the reason why the Serbs, who were members of Mr. Racan's party, including you, moved from that party to the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was one of the important reasons. The party, SDP, party of democratic changes, for which we voted, did not do anything about the changes. They simply kept observing it and it was one of the reasons why the Serbs decided to opt for another political party in order to better be able to articulate and protect their interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In June of 1990, was there an association created, an association of municipalities in northern Dalmatia and Lika?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. I believe that several municipalities got together and established an association of municipalities of northern Dalmatia and Lika.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that on the 25th of July 1990, a large assembly of Serbs from Croatia was held, attended by many people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, was a declaration on autonomy passed proclaiming or declaring autonomy of the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the Serb National Council established at that time?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was a decision adopted to schedule a referendum on the Serb autonomy?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was adopted to organise the referendum for determining cultural autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was this referendum held, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think that referendum for cultural autonomy was held immediately following that. It was held solely in the territory of this association of municipalities. Later on, I think in 1991, the second referendum was held where people had to vote for remaining within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the first referendum was scheduled for the 19th of August 1990? Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that it was held on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So it was held on that day?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was supposed to be held on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the reaction of Croatian authorities to the decision taken at the referendum?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The then leaders of Croatia said that they would prevent this referendum from being held, that it was unacceptable for them, and they said that they would use their services and institutions to prevent it from taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether certain steps were taken in relation to police stations employing Serbs in the territory of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they wanted to change the personnel makeup and that they wanted to introduce new symbols, new emblems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document, Exhibit P5, be placed on the ELMO? The text of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have before you, Mr. Dzakula, the words uttered by the Accused, Mr. Martic, to a journalist of Croatian television; is that correct? Do you recognise the text?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in English. I do not understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I read out this text to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, this is a text which noted down the words of Mr. Martic from the videotape. Mr. Martic is recorded as saying, "Say in your report that this is the people's police, that this police is protecting the people, and is against the Croatian government which threatens it." Do you remember this statement of Mr. Martic? It was put to you earlier.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to hear the previous words uttered on that tape, where the journalist of the Croatian television explains why he had come to Knin and why he was addressing the Serb policemen?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please remind me of that text?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Defence received from the Prosecution the transcript of that tape, and, above the words of Mr. Martic, there is the text that I'm going to read to you. "We came here to hear either confirmation or denial of the meeting held near Knin, in Cetina where it was requested that Yugoslavia and Serbia, as the mother states protect Serbian people from Croatian police." These are the words uttered by the reporter of the Croatian television. The warning was also sent out to the Sibenik police, to the Secretariat of the interior, as well as to the police stations in Drnis and Cin [phoen], saying that they would be fired upon without warning if they failed to stop vehicles travelling to Knin. The Sibenik police knows nothing about this information. However, they confirmed that there were barricades erected on the roads leading to Strmica and Badjani [phoen]. In yesterday's statement, President of the Knin municipality called the events in Petrinja and the confiscation of weapons belonging to reserve police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, are you still quoting or are you now speaking from the bar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quoting the entire time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because according to the record, the quotation was closed after "Croatian police." "We came here to here either confirmation or denial of the meeting held near Knin in Cetina where it was requested that Yugoslavia and Serbia as the mother states protect Serbian people from Croatian police." Closed quotation. From then on, the quotation is -- there is no quotation. And then are you saying, when you continue to say, these are the words uttered by the reporter of the Croatian television, that's still part of the quotation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I never once said that the quotation ended. I apologise, if I was imprecise. This whole time I've been reading out the words uttered by the journalists which precede Mr. Martic's statement. So this entire time I've been quoting the words uttered by the reporter. As --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- delivered to us by the Prosecution and their transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In which case then, you say the closed quotation mark after Croatian police must be deleted and what you have been saying up until I interrupted you is still part of the quotation? And I think can those who type for us please take note of that? Okay. You may proceed with your quotation, Mr. Milovancevic, and may the typists please note that that is a quotation of what we are going to be saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, with respect, I believe it's still not accurate. On reading the transcript I believe the quotation should open at the warning. There is one sentence in between where Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat it again. On my reading of the transcript, there is one sentence where counsel for the Defence is explaining that this is part of the transcript. Rather, this is part of what was uttered by the reporter. It should pick up again and open the quotation at the warning, which is a continuation of what was said. That would record it correctly, I believe. Is that so, counsel? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely right, Your Honour. Indeed, at one point in time I inserted my comment. I just wanted to re-emphasise that I was reading the words of the journalist and following that, quotation picks up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me conclude the text. I apologise for the text being so lengthy. So we broke off at the last sentence, I'm quoting: "In yesterday's statement, President of Knin municipality called the events in Petrinja and the confiscation of weapons belonging to reserve police force a continued state terror against the Serb people in Croatia, and called the people to defend their autonomy and freedom." End of quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, immediately following this text, Mr. Martic gave a statement to the journalist, the one that was shown to you, where he says, "Tell the people that this is the people's police, that its job is to defend the people against Croatian government." My question is: Is there a link between the events, namely the one when Croatian police confiscated the weapons of the reserve police on one hand, and on the other hand, the attitude, the behaviour of Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you -- what you have in mind is the events in Petrinja and the situation that they wanted to prevent in Knin, then, yes, this is probably what Mr. Martic had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. Can you tell us how did the Serbs in Croatia vote at the referendum for autonomy in 1990, the first referendum that was held?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that referendum was organised only partially. First the one for cultural autonomy which was organised in northern Dalmatia and Lika. I heard that a lot of people turned up to vote. However, I don't have much information about it. Especially not official information. I don't know whether there were any official lists or simply people showed up to vote, to express their opinion. I can given you more information about the second referendum held on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We will get to that one as well. Is it true that in late December 1990, Croatia adopted a new condition where the Serbs were no longer a nation but became a national minority, an ethnic minority. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Croatia adopted a new constitution. The Serbs ceased to be a constituent people and became an ethnic minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that one day previously, there had been an answer to the amendments to the Croatian constitution whereby the SAO Krajina was proclaimed with a new statute?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is this late in 1990 and more specifically the 21st of December 1990?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was late in 1990. I can say that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the status of the SAO Krajina according to this document dated late 1990? Did this imply autonomy within the boundaries of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's as far as I remember at least. That's the way it was termed, an autonomous district, a region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the Spegelj film and Croatia arming itself, what was going on in early 1991? Was Croatia beginning to arm itself? Did you have any information on that?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard from a variety of people that they were arming themselves, but we didn't see this for ourselves. Therefore I can't tell you how this was done but there were lots of stories in circulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about an increase in the number of Croatian police officers? Was this the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the general numbers of police presence were increased, in order to change the ethnic makeup of the police force. This was suggested at the time. I think roughly 40 new police officers were sent to Pakrac as part of this initiative because there needed to be an act compensation. The belief was that there were too few Croats and too many Serbs in Pakrac working for the police. That's what the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Croatia believed and this is how they decided to compensate town by town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Alongside with the police force were the numbers increased also in the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- their units were reviewed soon after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you say that this was a new Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is usually believed to be its beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in late February 1991, Croatia adopted a decision that the federal laws would no longer apply in its territory, assuming upon itself all the competencies of the -- and powers of the federal authorities?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. It was on the 21st of February 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the reaction was of Croatia's Serbs when this decision became known?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were quite stunned and certainly not pleased. The Serbs believed Yugoslavia to be a state of all its citizens and everybody had a fine life in Yugoslavia. This was something entirely new to them and something they by no means expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about the 28th of February 1991? Did the SAO Krajina adopt a decision to separate from Croatia for this very reason?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date but I know that this decision was taken in late February or early March, sometime around then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You've already referred to what happened in Pakrac on the 1st of March 1991.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Croatian government sent its police officers into Pakrac and that they brought back automatic rifles to take home? Can you please explain what happened?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in late February, when reinforcements arrived made up of about 40 new police officers with new insignia on their caps. In Pakrac there were two police stations at the time. One bore the old insignia and one bore the new, changed insignia. Based on information received from the then chief of police, Jovo Vezmar suggesting that the new police officers who had arrived were taking weapons from the police station and taking weapons home, there was a proposal by the president of the municipal assembly of Pakrac, Milan Bozic, and his colleague, president of the executive board, and they ordered the chief of police to disarm those new police officers who came in bearing the new sets of insignia and to dismiss them. They also said that he should summon all the reserve police officers from previous lists and enlist their assistance, get them involved, which is exactly the course of action that he took, which provided a motive for the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia to send in their Special Forces to Pakrac in order to free the police officers who had been disarmed and to re-establish control over the Pakrac police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dzakula. Can you tell us how exactly they re-established full control?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had announced their arrival, as far as I remember. They drove in APCs and looked prepared for some serious operations. They came from several directions, a number of reserve police officers had been summoned. Many of the local Serb males from the area also got involved, some armed and some unarmed. Roadblocks were established along the road to Pakrac because they wanted to prevent the measures being taken by the Croatian police. During the night a JNA unit arrived in Pakrac and entered the police station, asking the police to have the barricades and roadblocks removed and saying that they would be offering protection from clashes. Once the police had followed suit, the JNA allowed the APCs carrying Croatian Special Forces to enter Pakrac in the early morning hours. Soon after, there was a shootout between the new Croatian police officers and the active and reserve police officers belonging to Pakrac municipality. The shootout lasted for about one or one and a half hours, there was a lull then, and the former Pakrac police or the Serb police, if I can call it that way, was moved out of town or expelled from town while the new police forces were installed, those that had arrived from Zagreb. Some people were arrested in the aftermath and released several days later, which is when the army came in as well as representatives of the Zagreb-based authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This was a very detailed description, Mr. Dzakula, but when you talk about APCs are you talking about APCs that the Croatian police officers were firing from?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were arriving in police APCs. Some of them were APCs, yes. Were they firing from them? Well, probably from them too, not that I can say myself. I didn't see this but I heard that they were firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if on that occasion the JNA was fired on as well?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the next day or perhaps that evening. The JNA APC came under fire by the Croatian police, but no fire was returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Following these events in Pakrac, did anything happen, as far as the work of Yugoslavia's Presidency was concerned? Was there a request to declare a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, attempts were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. That's fine. I apologise. Was a state of emergency eventually declared?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We have been speaking so far about what happened in Pakrac on the 1st of March 1991. The first thing of note that happened after there was the Plitvice incident on the 31st of March and 1st of April 1991. You explained that on the 31st of March there was an SDS meeting at Plitvice, didn't you or rather Obrovac?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 31st of March there was a meeting of the main and executive boards of the SDS in Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was it not agreed at this meeting to adopt a strategy to negotiate and to conciliate with the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a long session and a decision was taken to try to negotiate with the Croatian authorities and to adopt a conciliatory approach. A groundwork was laid, if you like, for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any contacts with the Croatian authorities in order to achieve this?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had announced this meeting that was to be held on the 31st of March, and I had also announced what the nature of the meeting would be and what the decision to be taken was. This had been announced, therefore. I don't know exactly when the session ended but I know that the party president, Jovan Raskovic announced this new decision. I'm not sure if it was sent to the media or if it reached anyone at the time. There is no way I can know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the next day, the 1st of April 1991? Did the Croatian authorities dispatch two busloads of police officers to Plitvice to take over the Serb police station? Was this perhaps on the 31st? I may be wrong about the dates.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the morning hours of the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this a holiday, a bank holiday of some kind?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Orthodox Easter, as far as I remember, a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think we could call this an attack by the Croatian police against the Serb police officers on Serbian Easter of all days?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody takes up weapons, then perhaps you could speak of an attack, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Mr. Hadzic also attended the meeting at Obrovac, that he also was in favour of this peaceful position, conciliatory position but that he was arrested by the Croatian police during this mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you not also explain that Mr. Hadzic, for as long as he was being held by the Croatian police, was beaten black and blue?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was physically beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that regarding the situation in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May 1992, so far we have been talking about the 1st of April and now we are talking about the 2nd of May 1992. Is it true that there had been negotiations with the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you helped with the negotiations surrounding the release of Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved, and I went to meet him when he was eventually released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any barricades in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that after your negotiations with the Croatian authorities, you brought your influence to bear on the local Serbs to have the barricades removed?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did go to speak to the locals and I told them to get the barricades off the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did they listen to you?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was -- what was the reaction of the Croatian side on the 2nd of May 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the morning hours, or sometime during that day, I think a busload of police officers drove into Borovo Selo. Fire was opened and there was a clash between the locals of Borovo Selo on the one hand and the Croatian police forces on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was anyone killed?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The media reported that a number of police officers were killed, but that some of the Serbs, too, were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think we understand each other. When you say "police officers," whose police officers do you mean?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were on the bus which arrived in Borovo Selo but also some Serbs, both police officers and civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA step in to do something about this, to keep the clashes from spreading?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA appeared on the scene to keep the conflict from spreading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We talked about what happened on the 2nd of May. Was a referendum scheduled in Croatia for May 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Croatian government scheduled a referendum on secession from Yugoslavia. There was another one scheduled by the SAO Krajina, a referendum on staying within Yugoslavia. Therefore, two parallel referenda were held within a week, you might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are still in May 1992. Were there any changes in Yugoslavia's Presidency, more specifically was Stjepan Mesic not appointed or elected president of the Yugoslav Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a bit of a tug of war and, after some time, Stjepan Mesic became --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt but just for clarity on the record, I think all of these questions have been about 1991 but occasionally, there is reference to 1992 and it just has happened again. So just to clarify that all these -- if it could be clarified that all these events we have been talking about are in fact in 1991, including this last event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that so, Mr. Milovancevic? Is it a mistake to refer to 1992 here? Should it be 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If 1992 was mentioned, then it's definitely a mistake. We have been referring continuously to the events from March, April, and May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at page 27 of the transcript, the question by you says, Thank you. "We are still in May 1992. Were there any changes in Yugoslav's Presidency, more specifically was Stjepan Mesic not appointed or elected president of the Yugoslav Presidency," so you're referring to 1992 there. Should it be 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A slip of tongue. Yes, Your Honours, it should have been 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. And thank you to you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to understand the election of Mr. Mesic to that post, please tell us, Mr. Dzakula, the Presidency was a collective organ?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a collective organ of six republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that each republic nominated its president when their turn came?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So we are now referring to May 1991, when it was turn for Croatia to nominate its representative and have him elected as president of the Presidency, this collective organ; is that correct, Mr. Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Mesic was not elected or appointed when his turn came, that there were certain problems concerning that.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because his nomination was challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was there pressure exerted by the European Community and the United States following which Stjepan Mesic was appointed president of the Presidency of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. Following the pressure exerted by them, Mr. Stjepan Mesic was appointed president of the Presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that a representative of the Republic of Croatia was appointed head of state, the same Croatia that earlier, several months before that, declared that none of the federal laws would hence forth apply in its territory and that in May declared that it was seceding from the federal state, it was declared after a referendum?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. But under the pressure exerted by the European Community, the results of that referendum were supposed to enter into force only several months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We will get to that later. Can you tell us how long did Stjepan Mesic remain president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could be wrong, but I think it was sometime until the fall, until October of 1991. I don't know the exact date. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember a sentence uttered by Stjepan Mesic upon his return to Zagreb, to the capital of Croatia? He stated this in the Croatian assembly after he stopped being president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the sentence was, "I have accomplished my task. I have destroyed Yugoslavia." Something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I were to correct you and say that his words were, "I have accomplished my task. Yugoslavia ceased to exist. It is no more."

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that your words are more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in view of our new schedule is this a good time for a break, if we are going to adhere to this one hour 15 minute session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it's convenient for the Defence, we shall take the break at this stage. Thank you very much. Court will adjourn and reconvene on the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we continue with the cross-examination of the witness, let me just mention that the Chamber has got feedback from the interpreters that, one, they are thankful for the Chamber considering their concerns and that they really haven't got any preference for the one or the other time schedule. We therefore stick to the time schedule that we've agreed on, one hour 15 minutes at a time. They are, however, particularly grateful for the 30-minute break that we are being given because it affords them sufficient time to rest and we are grateful to them for their input. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back, Mr. Dzakula, to the 2nd of May 1991. We spoke about the events in Borovo Selo. Do you know what happened in Zadar on the 2nd of May 1991? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you are referring to the personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the setting of fire and demolition of some premises in Zadar on the 2nd of May 1991? If not, just tell us so.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the speech given by General Tudjman in Trogir on the 5th of May 1991, in which he called upon the Croatian people to stage a rebellion against the JNA, following which the events in Split ensued?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, did you watch on television, the events which took place in Split on the second day after that speech given by Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember is that a group of citizens attacked a military personnel carrier. I think that they tore off and broke weapons, that they grabbed a soldier and pulled him by his head and his neck, and I think that there were even some casualties on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When I say to you that on that occasion the TV cameras recorded how they strangled a soldier called Sasko Gesovski, who died then, would that be true?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, we are still dealing with May of 1991. Following all of these events, could the entire situation in Croatia be described as a situation in which the Serbs were harassed, their houses set on fire, they themselves were taken in for interviews in police stations?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were taken into custody, they were provoked, they were attacked, but right now I wouldn't be able to say that that was a mass occurrence that took place on a large scale, as you have put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where that happened, where did they arrest people, take them into custody? Were there any cases of people disappearing?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not only in May. It was just before summertime, sometime in June, before the events in Vukovar. I heard that people went missing, I heard that there were provocations, that people were called on telephone and threatened. There were such cases in Pozega. I know for a fact that this did take place and, as for the rest, I only heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that Croatia and Slovenia unilaterally declared their independence, seceded from Yugoslavia on the 25th of June 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. I wouldn't be able to confirm or deny the date that you mention but I know, however, that they did adopt a decision to secede from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened in Slovenia after Slovenia, together with Croatia, simultaneously with Croatia, decided to secede and become independent?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the TO of Slovenia wanted to take over a customs offices on the border, following which a conflict erupted between the JNA and Slovenian Territorial Defence. This conflict lasted for several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Following these clashes, did the JNA, the federal army, withdraw from Slovenia following the orders issued by the leadership of the country, in order to avoid further escalation of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. The JNA withdrew from Slovenia in accordance with the order of the president of the Presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm sorry. Your Honour, I'm wondering with respect to these questions which are getting quite far afield, if we could have a basis for the knowledge. Is -- are these things he knows about because he heard about them or witnessed them or -- I don't know. Just wondering if we could have a basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response to that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am putting these questions to the witness, and I can be more specific if necessary, but so far, I've been putting questions about events which were reported on by all the media at the time, radio, television, press. This was the topic of the day, something that was discussed by the general public, by every citizen, so I'm just asking the witness about the events and whether he remembers them. We are not going into the analysis of the events, legal analysis, no. We are just trying to establish these events, the fact that they took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do understand, Mr. Milovancevic. Can I just confer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed with your cross-examination, Mr. Milovancevic. If you can -- if it's possible to narrow your questions it will be appreciated, but we understand that the witness also was a bit at large during examination-in-chief, and he was telling us about incidents that he read about, that he heard from other people, that he heard from the media, and that to some extent you are also entitled to canvass in those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When we touched upon the events which took place in March and April, you mentioned that there was a decision which was suspended, a decision on independence. So we will now revert so that. You told us that Croatia and Slovenia in June of 1991 adopted a decision to secede from Yugoslavia. Would the term "the Brioni moratorium" mean anything to you, it was in place from the 8th of July 1991 for three months onwards?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that document. I think the document prescribed that the result of the referendum would be postponed by three months, would be postponed from implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that this moratorium pertained to the decision taken by Slovenia and Croatia on secession and that this was arranged between the European Community, Croatia, Slovenia, and the Yugoslav state?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's how it was arranged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, do you know something about the events which took place in late August in the vicinity of Cavtat and Gradus? Did you hear about any action taken by the ZNG in that area?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Reichl-Kir, does that name ring a bell? And if so, would you tell us anything you know about that.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That name is quite well known in Croatia. Reichl-Kir was the chief of police in Osijek. He led negotiations with the Serbs in Vukovar and the suburbs of Osijek. He tried to alleviate the fears that existed among the Serbs there, and he was killed in an ambush set up by Croatian extremists. It was set up for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about what happened with the Serbs in the summer and fall of 1991 in Sisak? Do you have any information concerning that?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that. And later on, through the years, that information was confirmed, namely that the Serbs went missing, some of them were found later in the Sava River, some were found in their homes, some of them had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly where Osijek is located, in which part of Croatia -- I apologise, I meant Sisak, not Osijek.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sisak is located in the centre of Croatia, in the area of Banija and Kordun. Sisak is surrounded by municipalities in which the Serbs were the majority. Vojnic, Vrgin Most, Glina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, when, as you say, Serbs went missing, were killed, were beaten, were there any armed conflicts in Sisak or not?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no armed conflicts in Sisak. These people went missing as civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Pakracka Poljana, Marino Selo, the events which took place in October and November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, we heard that there were prisons or camps in Pakraca Poljana and Marino Selo. This is in the territory of Pakrac municipality, towards Kutina. These were the locations to which the Serbs were taken and killed throughout the war. We still do not know the number of the people that perished there. Serbs from Zagreb and other places in Croatia were taken to Pakracka Poljana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened with the Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were beaten and killed. Some, who had been taken there, were never found again. All we flow is that they were taken there and now they are listed as missing. Some were released after a large amount was paid in bail. And then there were some who were released after their friends intervened. They were released and were free after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were these Serbs arrested with no relevant order from the Courts? Do you have any information on that, with no arrest warrants?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Serbs from these towns were arrested and taken away with no arrest warrants whatsoever. They would simply go missing and never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: A while ago we referred to the Brioni memorandum about suspending the independence decision for three months. Did you hear anything about the 21st of September 1991? This was in Karlovac, at the Korana bridge. Does this ring a bell, the Korana bridge and Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that is quite well known, in fact. It was at the Korana bridge that a clash occurred between, I think, the JNA soldiers on the one hand and the Croatian ZNG soldiers on the other. A number of soldiers were surrendered and subsequently killed at the bridge itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about this description? They were forced to lie down, face down. They were shot at, their throats were slit, some jumped and the perpetrators were eventually tried. Does this description fit what you knew about these events at the time?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is consistent with what I heard and read about in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the trial ever reached an end, the trial of these perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The case was retried because there had been apparently miscarriage of justice and there was a great amount of dissatisfaction with the sentence that was first reached. This is still ongoing, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We were talking about September 1991. Today, in 2006, this trial is still continuing?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, it has not been concluded yet. It is an ongoing trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us anything about the way the Croatian authorities, the police, and the paramilitary ZNG and the National Guards Corps viewed and treated the JNA. Just in order to please speed things up a little, please answer this and then I'll ask some other questions, too.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA was called upon to leave Croatia and to hand over their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about barracks being laid siege to, electricity supplies and water supplies being cut off, barracks being surrounded, soldiers being killed? Did you hear anything about these things or incidents?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about these things happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fate of some major barracks of the JNA in Slavonia, in areas such as Virovitica, Varazdin, and other places?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those barracks too were laid siege to. There were negotiations to surrender. Varazdin surrendered alongside with a very strong tank unit. In Bjelovar clashes wrote out. There was a major by rank, I think, who blew up himself and that part of the barracks, the part of the barracks he was positioned in. In Julica [phoen] the barracks were surrendered in Oljani [phoen]. The barracks was surrendered too, as was the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In there way, did the Croatian authorities and their armed units acquire large number of weapons and ordnance, artillery, large amounts of ammunition and military trucks and vehicles?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the barracks were handed over they acquired a significant amount of equipment, weapons and ammunition. I'm not familiar with specific numbers but I know that people talked about a lot of tanks and a lot of weapons that were in the barracks at the time. The whole thing was just taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about attacks occurring against military columns retreating from Slovenia. The state leadership had taken a decision for the JNA to withdraw from Croatia, they had to pass -- to withdraw from Slovenia they had to pass through Croatia on their way back. Were there any attacks? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know one military column was stopped in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened to their weapons?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it stayed in Croatia, the weapons did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can slow down, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember a conversation with Mr. Karadzic - this was in late October 1991 - concerning the situation in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about October 1991. Did you mention at the time that Western Slavonia was encircled?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention the fact that Western Slavonia was encircled or surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this conversation, did you mention the fact that General Uzelac, alongside with the 5th Corps of the JNA had attempted to break through the siege in order to rescue the women and children who were trapped inside?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the details. I may have said that. If this statement exists in any form I would like to go through it again. I know that there had been a break through and that Western Slavonia was annexed by the Republic of Serbia or rather Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, and that there was a convoy carrying women and children on their way out of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, which state was this being encircled in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have to provide a rather comprehensive answer. When the clashes first broke out on the 19th of August, and this had begun on the 14th in Okucani, the TO of Pakrac, Daruvar, Grubisno Polje, Slatina, Daruvar, and some other places held positions around the towns which I mentioned, where Serb villages predominated, with a number of Croatian villages dotted between them. The Okucani Territorial Defence was in charge of the area between Gradiska and Novska. For about 50 days the TO held these positions with no JNA assistance because the JNA only arrived later on. There was no contact with Bosnia-Herzegovina or with the remaining parts of Croatia. Fighting was going on between the TO on the one hand and the Croatian police units on the other. Throughout, there were wounded who were dying because no doctors were at hand to help them. Nobody came. Not even the military helicopters arrived in the area at the time, in order to evacuate the wounded. We had Croatian police forces around us throughout, the ZNG or the army. I'm not sure if they were called the army at the time or just ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the JNA stepped in in order to break through the encirclement and rescue the women and children, does this mean that the JNA went in, in a manner of speaking, to help the surrounded Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had been expected that the JNA would arrive in order to put an end to the clashes, in order to establish a confrontation line between the then Serb TO and the Croatian police. The JNA only got as far as Okucani and Bijela Stijena in order to open a corridor to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Throughout the war in Western Slavonia the farthest point they reached was Pakrac. They never went anywhere further than that. A line had been established near Novska and Nova Gradiska, and that's where the fighting occurred between the army and the Serb TO on the one hand, and the Croatian police and the ZNG on the other. The territory beyond Pakrac and as far as Slatina Daruvar and Grubisno Polje was covered by the local TO members from those municipalities and those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If we could please display on the ELMO Defence Exhibit 1D00-0001?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that an exhibit number or an ERN number, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received here in court a number for this exhibit. The lower number may be 00307122. And our exhibit is marked 1D00-0001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We'll bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the document there, sir?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is the English document, or a document in English, produced by the command of the 5th military district, the JNA military district. It's in reference to a genocide against the Serbs, and this was sent to the leaders of the ECMM for the former Yugoslavia. I will quote you a portion of this document. "Starting from 1st of November 1991, the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia have carried out an all-out assault on the territories of Western Slavonia and Moslavina."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I just wonder if there could first be some establishment whether the witness has any knowledge about this document generally or information about it or can authenticate it or anything before the document is just read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was this document not handed over by the Prosecution, as Mr. Milovancevic said?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. Of course, it was handed over by the Prosecution but in -- along with thousands of other documents, and I'm -- all I'm suggest something that I'm not sure that the witness has any knowledge about this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic? Would you like to establish whether the witness does have any knowledge of the document before you ask him about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, at the time in question, mid-1991, were you aware of numerous communiques produced by the JNA regarding the situation prevailing in the country?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of a number of reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In these announcements and reports, was the situation throughout the country addressed, as well as the situation in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about what you heard in the media as well?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'll be showing you a document now which is in relation to that period in time. What I want to know is whether the substance of this document reflects the situation as we were aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Chamber's leave, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So, what we see here is the command of the 5th military district of the JNA informing the European Community. Here we see Andrija Raseta, the deputy commander, Lieutenant General Andrija Raseta. He says, "Starting from the 1st of November 1991, the armed forcers of the Republic of Croatia have carried out an all-out assault against the territories of Western Slavonia and Moslavina. The target of this assault are the inhabitants of Serbian ethnicity who make up a majority of the inhabitants in the general region of Grubisno Polje. It has been established beyond dispute that the following villages have been demolished or burned. Velika and Mala Peratovica, Mio Kovicevo, Veliki and Mali Grdjevac, Velika Dapcevica, Sibenik, and Gakovo."

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to claims made by the refugees, the same fate befell the following villages as well: Velika and Mala Barna, Topolovica, Kovacica, Donja Rasenica, as well as six others. In the area of Djakovo" --

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gakovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Gakovo. "The Croatian armed forces have set fire to a forest, the total area of which is 630 acres, in which there were over a thousand refugees. It is assumed that these people died in the fire. Irrespective of the -- or, rather, apart from the refugees in the general area of Banja Luka, some 4.000 persons, there are around 10.000 or more Serb refugees around the mountains in the Psunj and Papuk areas. For the most part, these are the sick, elderly, women, and children. Due to the lack of food and medicines as well as the extremely cold weather, these people are facing an extremely critical situation. Those inhabitants who have not escaped by this time were killed."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, end of quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The information contained in this department, is this consistent with something that you as someone who hails from the area were aware of?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I happened to be in the area when this exodus from Grubisno Polje occurred. This started on the 15th of October. This was because of the fighting that had erupted involving the TO, who left the Grubisno Polje area along with their families and fled. The villages they left behind were burnt down, as well as any remaining civilians. But what you said about 1.000 people dying in that fire, I don't think that was the case. I don't think there were as many people in the woods to begin with. They had been evacuated. There were individual persons left who stayed behind, such as the elderly or handicapped people, and I don't think those people made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this exhibit, this report, into evidence, Your Honours, as an exhibit of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure -- I would object to its admission. The witness has said that the document is not accurate, and to the extent there is information in the document, that he has confirmed portions of it, he's testified about that and I don't see why the document that's written by somebody else that -- and it has not been established that he has any knowledge about this document or bout the author of the document, I'm not sure what it adds. But most importantly he states that it's not accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But is this a document that was provided by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was, but not in context of this witness. The Prosecution provides thousands of documents in -- that have some relationship to the case.
