That doesn't -- the -- and the Prosecution obtains documents from all kinds of sources. The fact that we provided it isn't any vouching for its accuracy or its authenticity or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What would be the purpose of providing it, Mr. Whiting, if the Prosecution doesn't want it used? I mean, obviously this document does not originate from any source within the control of the Defence. It originates from a source within the control of the Prosecution, and if the Defence has it, are they not entitled to ask any witness that the Prosecution calls about it? They don't know in respect of which witness the Prosecution intends using this document. They have a witness before them, and they want to establish if he knows anything about the contents of it, and if he agrees with some parts of it and disagrees with other parts, does that make the document not admissible?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I would suggest that the Court has put two different questions out on the table. The first is the most important one in some sense because it touches on all the documents that may come in in this trial. The Prosecution under the Rules of disclose has provided documents on its exhibit list which it intends to move into evidence but it has also provided thousands of pages of documents under its other disclosure obligations, most predominantly including Rule 68. Those, under the Rules and under the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, the Prosecution's obligated to provide those documents regardless of whether it has any information about their authenticity and the Prosecution obtains documents from all kinds of sources and if, on its face, it has information that might be relevant to the Defence or might be arguably Rule 68, it gets sent over to the Defence. That is no -- the fact that it is in the possession of the Prosecution is not a -- is no vouching for its authenticity or its reliability or anything. The Prosecution has plenty of documents in its collection which, I can state, are not reliable. Now, so the mere fact that it has been provided by the Prosecution, we would submit, is not a basis for admission under the Rules into evidence in this trial. The second point, however, Your Honour has raised, that the witness, of course, has confirmed certain portions of the document and on that basis, I defer to the Court on whether the Court will allow admission simply on that basis. I will take that argument no further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the first point, Mr. Whiting, the only problem that the Chamber has is that you are arguing that the fact that it is provided by the Prosecution doesn't mean that the Prosecution vouches for its authenticity. Now, if the Prosecution, as the producer of the document, cannot vouch for its authenticity, the question from the Bench becomes, how much more difficult is it for the Defence to vouch for its authenticity? This is a document that they have received, and according to the Defence, this is a document that the Prosecution intends using at some stage or another. And they've got a witness of the Prosecution before them and they want to check what it is that that witness knows about this document. How can the Defence vouch for its authenticity, if the producer of the document himself is not able to vouch for its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not at this moment able to confirm whether this document is a document that we intend to use. I haven't checked to see if it's in fact on our exhibit list. But the point I was making is that we have provided a large number of documents that are not on our exhibit list and the mere fact this we have provided it, maybe nobody can authenticate it. Maybe it's not authentic. But it is certainly not the jurisprudence of the Tribunal that because we have produced a document, that it is then -- the Defence -- it is -- then that is a basis for admission into evidence in the trial. That's -- I fail to -- I don't see the connection between the two things. The evidence for admission into the trial requires relevance -- requires a showing of relevance and some degree of authenticity or something, and perhaps that's been shown here but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Two points. Let's take a step back. You say that you -- the Prosecution produced a lot of documents and disclosed because of its obligation to disclose. What is the purpose of that disclosure? Number 1. Number 2, on the question of relevance, does the fact that the witness does confirm some of the contents of the document not relate to its relevance to the extent that the Defence conducts its case and wants to show how it relates to their case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the first point, the Prosecution, under the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, is required, under the Rules, to turn over any document or any evidence which, on its face, is potentially exculpatory. And moreover, under the new system of disclosure, the electronic disclosure suite, what in fact the Prosecution does is simply makes available to the Defence all of its documents that is within its collection, without necessarily an individual review or an individual determination of its relevance to this case. So the fact is the Defence has available to it through the electronic disclosure suite an enormous number of documents, many of which have nothing to do with this case. Nothing to do with this case. It is made available to the Defence so -- because we cannot know exactly what their defence is and so the whole -- the way that disclosure is done is the whole collection is made available to them and then they are able to search through to find documents which they believe will be relevant for their defence. And it's just necessarily part of the process that an enormous number of documents get turned over, both because of this requirement that even if it's on its face arguably exculpatory, it gets turned over, and because we, out of -- the process is to turn over just the whole collection to let them search through it, it then follows that the Defence is -- has available to it documents which don't necessarily relate to this case or have nothing to do with this case or cannot be authenticated for purposes of this case, which is why I'm pressing the point that there is no connection whatsoever between the fact that the document has an ERN number on it and comes from the Prosecution, and its relevance or authenticity for purposes of there case. So that's the first point. On the second point, I think -- I concede that an argument can be made that if the witness can confirm certain portions of the document, that perhaps on that basis it can be relevant, and there I would defer to the court on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the first point, Mr. Whiting, can you please guide this Chamber on the jurisprudence of this Tribunal on the purpose for disclosing documents and turning them over to the Defence in terms of Rule 68? When the Defence find any document that they want to use under -- from those documents that were turned over in terms of Rule 68 how are they supposed to proceed to tender that document into evidence? A document that does not originate from them, does not originate from their witness, and they get from the Prosecution, how are they -- in terms of the jurisprudence of this Court, how are though supposed to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me address both parts the question. The first part of the question, as I understand it, is what is the purpose for disclosing documents and turning them over to the Defence in terms of Rule 68? There are -- there are essentially two parts of Rule 68 as it has been amended in the last, I believe, year or 18 months. There is documents that in the actual knowledge of the Prosecution are -- arguably contain exculpatory evidence, must be turned over. And there, the Prosecution is -- even if, for example, if we got a document that said that Milan Martic was living on the moon during 1991 and 1992, we would have to turn that over. We are not allowed to determine, well, that's false or that's obviously not true. The Rules -- the jurisprudence of the Tribunal says, even if it's on its face, no matter how crazy it might seem or obviously untrue, we -- it's our obligation to turn that over and that's all we do. That's the first part of Rule 68. The second part of Rule 68 is -- contains a provision which refers to the electronic disclosure suite in which -- and what we do as a way of making this process of disclosure more complete and more expeditious is that we just put on an electronic collection an entire -- all the documents that have been obtained by the Prosecution, from all kinds of sources. Witnesses who are reliable, collections, all kinds of places these documents come in, millions of them, and the Defence has access to those and can search them and use them as it wishes. The second -- so that's how documents get disclosed and there is no purpose. It's just they get disclosed. Especially in the second category, they are just disclosed. They are made available with no purpose. It's to them to decide if there is anything beneficial in there. With respect to the second point, well, what is the Defence supposed to did a with a document that it obtains from the Prosecution. The Defence is under an obligation just like the Prosecution to have a witness or -- I'm getting a signal to slow down -- to have a witness or some other means of bringing the evidence that the document into the courtroom and getting it admitted into evidence. The threshold for that, of course, is lower than in many of our home jurisdictions, in terms of authenticity. Documents come in much more easily in this Tribunal. The threshold is quite low. However, there is nonetheless a showing that must be made and it's the same showing for the Prosecution and for the Defence. They have to have a witness or some other means to say this document is either authentic or reliable. It cannot be the case that it simply comes in because we have -- we have given them access to it. I hope I've been thorough or clear in my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've confused me further. You are saying to me, Rule 68 is purposeless and I cannot understand that. There must be a purpose for every Rule that's in the rule book. Otherwise, why is the Rule in the rule book? That's the first confusion that the Chamber has. The next is when you say that the threshold is lower in this Tribunal than it is in national jurisdictions, I find you in fact setting the threshold higher because -- of course, we come from different national jurisdictions. Where I come from, if a document came from the one party, obviously the other party -- it's disclosed. The other party has the right to use it without having to authenticate it. Now, you want them to authenticate it so you're putting -- from my experience you're putting the threshold higher, and I'm finding it logically and physically impossible for a party who received a document from another party to authenticate it, when in fact the originating party is unable to authenticate it. And I don't know how it is expected of the Defence to authenticate this document, because all they know is that it comes from the Prosecution. They are putting the document to a Prosecution witness, and if this witness happens to be the witness who provided this document, he will then answer the questions on it. If he's not the one, he will say I know nothing about this document and I'm not able to comment on anything that is contained in that document. Up until the witness who may have provided it comes up and he can then say, yes, I know that document and hopefully it can be authenticated that way. If it has to be authenticated at all. But how the Defence is supposed to know which Prosecution witness they must use to authenticate a document that comes from the Prosecution, from the way you explained the jurisprudence, I find it very difficult and impossible to accomplish, and I would like you to help me cross that little bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour. I certainly did not -- with respect to the first point, I certainly did not mean to suggest in any way that Rule 68 is purposeless. All that I was trying to say is that when we disclose a document or we make available, is a more accurate way to say it, a document or a collection of documents to the Defence, there is no suggestion in that act of making it available that we vouch for the document, that we think it's authentic or anything. And that is the sense in which I said it has no purpose. We don't -- we are not saying that it is -- if we make them allow them access to the document we are not saying it's relevant to there trial or that we think -- we have received it and we are making it available to them. So the Rule obviously has a purpose. The Rule obviously has a purpose, and that is to give the Defence access to all the documents that we have in our collection, and then in particular, any documents that come to our attention that are in our actual knowledge, contain Rule 68 information or potentially exculpatory information. With respect to the threshold showing, Your Honour is correct that we -- our national jurisdictions have different rules. In my jurisdiction, if the Prosecution provides a document, unless the Prosecution says this is an exhibit in the case that the Prosecution is going to use, or somehow in some other way ties it to the case, the fact that the Prosecution provides it to the Defence does not in my jurisdiction, to whatever extent this is relevant, that would not automatically allow for its admission in the trial. The Prosecution is not saying that it cannot authenticate this exhibit, this document, it's just saying it has not done so, or not to my knowledge, we have not done so, not our burden to authenticate the exhibit. If they want to use the exhibit, it's their burden to authenticate it through the witness. And they do it -- the Court has asked how do they do it? They do it the same way we do it. Through witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me venture what I -- in my understanding the purpose of Rule 68 is. In my understanding the purpose of Rule 68 is that whatever is disclosed is put at the disposal of the Defence to use in court, in prosecuting their case to the best of their ability in the defence of their client. In other words, where the Prosecution has exculpatory documents within their possession, they are obliged by the Rules to turn that information over to the Defence so that the Defence may use it in court. Not necessarily to authenticate it, because it is impossible for them to authenticate it, unless, of course, the Prosecution would say to them -- I see you shaking your head. I'm giving you what I -- my understanding of Rule 68 is and it may very well be wrong. I understand that. All I'm saying is that, to me, seems to be the logical and reasonable purpose, because where -- even in national jurisdictions this is the case, where the Prosecution has information that's exculpatory, they are obliged to turn that over to the Defence and not hide -- not hide it from them. And, of course, the Defence -- what would be the reason for turning it over if not to be used? Obviously, the Defence is supposed to use it to say, well, here is a document that we get from the Prosecution and this does say, in fact, we are not as guilty as you allege. It exculpates pats us. Otherwise there would be no purpose. To say the purpose is to turn it over, I'm saying what is the purpose of turning over? And the purpose of turning over is that that document be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The purpose is, assuming, as I think the question does, that the document that's turned over is in fact an exculpatory document, and just to be clear, that we've turned over many documents that in our view may not be exculpatory. But let's assume for a moment that the document turned over is in fact exculpatory on its face. It is -- nonetheless remains -- the Defence is able to use it but only if it can somehow bring it into evidence in the trial. Otherwise, I would suggest that the Defence could just bring a binders and binders of documents and just introduce them into evidence and say, well, recognition these are the exculpatory -- these are the documents that were provided to us by the Prosecution and here it comes into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think -- yeah, I think we are going into the realm of theory and speculation here. Mr. Whiting, I don't think that a document that says that, for example, and I'm being ridiculous here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A document that says Tony Blair is the Prime Minister of Britain, you wouldn't turn it over. It has nothing whatsoever to do with this case. The documents that have been turned over are documents that have, in the view of the Prosecution, have some relevance to this case. That is why the Prosecution turned them over. You don't turn over all documents that you come across since all your life.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's, Your Honour, I'm sorry, but that's just not correct. The Prosecution through the electronic disclosure suite makes available to the Defence all of the documents in its collection, and that includes documents which are relevant to this case, documents which are not relevant to this case. So my only point is that the mere fact that they have gotten the document from the EDS system, if that's where it's been obtained from, or -- and that it has an ERN number, does not say that the Prosecution has made a determination that it is relevant to the case. Moreover, even where -- even with respect to documents where the Prosecution has turned it over under the more specific provision of Rule 68, where the Prosecution -- the phrasing is -- actual, actual knowledge that the document or the information may be exculpatory, even when documents are turned over under that provision, where one might think, well, there the Prosecution has made a determination that it has relevance to the case, the Prosecution takes a very, very wide approach out of an abundance of caution, even in applying that Rule so that documents which have very tendentious relationships to this case or are only in a very convoluted way possibly exculpatory, out of an abundance of caution get turned over to the Defence. So again even under that Rule -- of course, there are some documents under that Rule that get turned over that we would concede are exculpatory and that have relevance to this case, and I'm not about to start fighting about those documents. But there are many documents even under that Rule that get turned over that we would suggest don't -- don't warrant admission into the trial particularly where you have a -- where you don't have -- where it's not authenticated. So I appreciate that in our -- one thing that I do think is in common in our jurisdictions, no doubt, is that when Rule 68 or whatever it's called in our jurisdictions gets turned over, there it probably does have something to do with the case and the argument there is quite different because it has -- it does have a connection to the case. But that's just not how it's done here, and so the Defence, if they produce a document that they -- that has an ERN number from the Prosecution, that doesn't mean that we've decided it has something to do with the case. I'm sorry, just one thing that has been provided to you -- to me that my colleague has confirmed that this document is in fact not on our exhibit list. We have not put it on our exhibit list as a document that we intend to introduce into the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But is it a document that you disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can't confirm that it's a document that we disclosed affirmatively under the first part of Rule 68 or that they had available to them under the electronic disclosure suite which is just a key to the library.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that but all I'm saying is this is a document that was disclosed by the Prosecution, by one or other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's absolutely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's correct, okay. Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any comments to make on the objection that is raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be brief, Your Honour. This is a document that was given to the Defence by the OTP. This is not a private document produced by a random individual. This comes from the highest possible military body, addressed to the head of the European Commission Monitoring Mission for the former Yugoslavia. There is reference leer to at least 16 or 17 villages. The authenticity of this information and the relevant time line was confirmed by the witness. There is nothing to compromise the substance of this report. It says here that a forest was set fire to in which there were refugees. There is an assumption being made that the people died in the fire. The witness is telling us that some did and some didn't. What we want to get from this document is the -- is general background and how civilians were treated, and this document paints the picture in no flattering terms. There is why the document is relevant to us. It is relevant to what the OTP themselves elicited from this witness. This is about events that the witness testified in chief about. I think the witness is well-placed to look at this document and its up to the Chamber to judge its probative value, and that is the reason we are using the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to tender the document through this witness or what do you want to do? And if so, I would invite you to proceed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our position is that this is certainly a document that we obtained from the OTP. The fact that it does not appear on the OTP exhibit list means nothing at this time because it speaks against the allegations made by the OTP. On the other hand the witness has confirmed the substance of this document for which reason I would now like to tender this document into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. This is an issue about which the Chamber would like to reflect, and maybe it is opportune at this stage to take our next break five minutes earlier and we will come back five minutes earlier so that we rule on the objection. Court adjourns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber has reflected on the jurisprudence of the Tribunal in matters of this nature, and has come to the decision, which is that the document will be admitted, and its probative value will be determined at a later stage. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, on a completely separate issue, I just -- I've had discussions with counsel, Defence counsel, about the schedule, and I think we both think it would be helpful if we had a discussion at the end, if we could just finish five minutes early and have a discussion about the schedule for this week in terms of the next witness, I think that would be productive for both parties and for the Chamber, and I think that Mr. Milovancevic would concur in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you say that discussion will take five minutes? If we stop at five to seven?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I guess since we are all lawyers, five -- can't do anything in five minutes so probably ten minutes would be more prudent, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You confirm, Mr. Milovancevic? Do you confirm, Mr. Milovancevic, ten minutes would be enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the only question is when will the Defence be able to complete our cross-examination? We have spent a lot of time discussing the exhibit and its introduction. If you could please take that into account too. I believe it is only once we have concluded our cross-examination that we can start considering other issues, with the Chamber's permission. That's all I'm saying. I'm not sure that we can tack that will tonight. That's all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say you're not sure if we can tackle what, the discussion that Mr. Whiting is talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if your understanding is that we should talk about it right now, there is no problem with that but what Mr. Whiting said was, conditionally, at the end of today's hearing. It's only that part of his sentence I'm talking about. I'm not sure I will be able to complete my cross-examination during today's session on account of all the time that we have lost discussing other issues. That's all I'm talking about. Other than that, I agree with my friend's proposal that we should perhaps take five or ten minutes to consider these other issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So that we don't delay further, I think the Chamber will then rule that that discussion will take place at the end of the cross-examination of this witness, before the re-examination, whenever that cross-examination ends, because in any case, the scheduling of following witnesses can only be determined after the final disposition with this witness. You may proceed with your cross-examination now, Mr. Milovancevic. Before you continue, can we give the exhibit the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit number 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please display the following document, Defence Exhibit 1D00-0041, and within that document, we have a highlighted portion. This is document 1D00-0043, and 44. This is on the B/C/S channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, can you see the order on your screen in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's right here and I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this order?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am. I was familiar with this at the time when all of this was happening in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this order is in reference to, what its substance is about?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see an English translation now but I will try to sum it up. An order was given --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If you will please excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour what I asked for is I'm not sure if it's possible but I asked for this document to be shown to the witness in his native tongue, 0043 is in English and 0044 is in B/C/S. There are two versions or copies, so that the witness may be able to read the document since he has no command of English whatsoever, if that can please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will the witness please be given the document in his language, 0044, please. Now it's given to me in 44, in English. Is it possible for the LiveNote to give it in English? I've got it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. Can you please tell us who issued this order?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was issued by the Defence Staff of Slavonska Pozega municipality, the Crisis Staff of Slavonska Pozega municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read this portion, item 1, of the order?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Carry out an evacuation of all citizens, their private property, clothes, shoes, bed linen, personal hygiene items, cutlery, basic lighting, jewels and money as well as livestock from the following areas, Oblakovac, Vucjak, Cecavacki, Jeminovac, Snjegavic" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please slow down a little bit?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Rasna, Pasikovci, Kujnik, Orljavac, Crljenci, Slobostina, Milivojevci, Podsrece, Vranic, Njezic, Pozeski Markovac, Klisa, Ozdakovci, Poljanska, Kantrovci, Gornji Vrhovci, Lucinci, and Oljasi, within 48 hours from the time this order takes effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dzakula. Can you please also read item 2 of this order?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The population will move to other villages in Slavonska Pozega municipality according to their own free choice. Those who have nowhere to go must speak to reception teams of the civil protection team for the evacuation in the areas of reception at the following locations: Ivandol, Dezevci, Perenci, Toranj and Buskupvci."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dzakula. Can you please be so kind and read item 3 of the order?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "This order enters into force on the 29th of October 1991 at 1200 hours. The time period during which this order shall be implemented shall depend on the circumstances in the stated area."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In item 4, are they banning any movement of the population upon the expiration of this deadline?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read to us the introductory part of this order? It gives reasons for its existence.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Lately, Chetnik terrorist forces and units of Yugoslav army have been threatening more and more with their combat activity the civilian population in the western portion of municipality of Slavonska Pozega. In order to protect the lives of residents and enable successful defence in that area, the Crisis Staff of Slavonska Pozega municipality hereby issues this order."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. Can you tell us to what portion of the population, namely population of what ethnicity, does this order pertain?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All villages in that area had Serb residents and residents left their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened with their villages? And where did the population go?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vast majority withdrew towards Pakrac and then continued on to Bosnia. Those who remained were mostly elderly and handicapped and they were killed. The houses were looted and set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As for the earlier events in that area and in other areas of Croatia, do you believe that these residents had any other choice but flee?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had no other choice. They had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender this document into evidence as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to the -- that one page going into evidence. I'd note that it's part of a -- there are 64 pages that are in that that are there that are -- that have been -- it's part of a 64-page document and my -- I assume he's just moving in that one page and that I have no objection to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That document, as displayed on the screen, will be admitted into evidence as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you already spoke how the JNA barracks were attacked. Did these attacks take place only in Slavonia or throughout Croatia? You probably heard about this on the -- from the media.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That took place throughout Croatia, wherever there were barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about 14 cease-fires or truces concluded between the JNA and Croatian leadership, attempting to reach a peaceful settlement?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that. We hailed each and every one of those truces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to refer to the October events of 1991. Does the last name Zec ring a bell, a family from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you know about the family and its fate?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The family was taken away by Croatian extremists employed in the police. They were taken to Sljeme mount. That's a mountain outside of Zagreb. The husband and the wife were killed, and the daughter was either raped and killed or just killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how old the girl was?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think she was 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't tell us about the ethnicity of this family.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any combat activities in Zagreb at that time?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were the perpetrators ever identified?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was done and they were investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that they were not convicted and that they were members of Mr. Tudjman's security detail?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, now we are going to turn to events having to do with the arrival of international forces. You gave evidence and said that on the 2nd of January 1992, the Vance Plan was signed. Is that correct? Did I quote your words correctly?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that on the 2nd of January in Sarajevo, a cease-fire was signed between the JNA and representatives of the Croatian army in order to implement the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the troops of the United Nations arrived in March of 1992. What is your basis for claiming that they arrived precisely in March?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my recollection. I can't be certain about it but I know that there were first preparations for their arrival and then they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the Vance Plan envisioned that the UN troops would be deployed to the Serb areas in Croatia where the Serb population constituted either a majority or a significant minority, and areas in which ethnic disagreements led to a conflict? Are you aware of this provision in the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the UN forces arrived in the first half of 1992. That's your recollection. Did you hear about a report of the former 5th Corps of the JNA stating that the Western Slavonia zone was handed over to the UN in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about an operation which took place on the Miljevac plateau? Did this take place on the 21st of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the operation on the Miljevac plateau but I can remember the exact date. I know that there was an operation there, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the Miljevac plateau in the area that was declared to be the UN safe area?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the armed forces of Croatia attack this area under the UN protection and did they kill a large number of members of the Serbian TO?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that the UN Security Council condemned this operation and ordered Croatia to withdraw from the occupied area?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of the following fact, namely that on that occasion the Croatian forces killed about 40-odd members of the Serbian TO and threw them into a pit?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For a long time, there were demands to unearth and locate these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the state in which the bodies of the victims were returned?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of the operation called Maslenica operation in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the Maslenica area under the UN protection?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the 21st of January 1993, did the Croatian army, together with the Special Forces, attack that area?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to the Serb villages in that area?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I don't remember the Maslenica events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember in general whether there were any victims or not?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was combat around Maslenica. I know there were victims but I don't know in exactly which settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did any Serb residents perish in the operation, if you remember that generally?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've told you, I heard that there had been combat, that there had been victims, people who were killed, and houses destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that the Security Council in relation to this operation of Croatian armed forces against the UN protected area, adopted a resolution condemning this and demanding the withdrawal of Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We mentioned the Maslenica operation which took place in January of 1993 onwards. The combat went on for quite a while, is it correct, Mr. Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You already gave evidence about the Daruvar agreement. Do you remember when it was concluded?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was signed on the 18th of February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained to us how you signed that agreement hoping to resolve the daily problems people were encountering; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in negotiations with the Croatian side, in addition to you, members of the UNHCR or UNPROFOR took part as well?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what was the substance of the Daruvar agreement?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was an expression of goodwill to create an atmosphere of tolerance, an atmosphere where problems with utilities would be resolved, electricity and water supply, because that had been cut off. That locations would be determined where friends and family members who had been separated during the war would be able to meet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. At the time when the Daruvar agreement was concluded, did you hold any post in the government of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was vice-Prime Minister of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that in order to reach agreement, you went covertly to that meeting without informing the assembly and the cabinet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Daruvar agreement contain a provision specifying under which terms the agreement would be made public?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was not to announce the text of the agreement on the media until it was confirmed by the Serb -- by the assembly of the Serbian region of Western Slavonia. Once they ratified it, then both sides were supposed to make the agreement public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you comply with that provision of the Daruvar agreement?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did the Croatian side do?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian side announced on the same day that Daruvar agreement had been signed and gave a wrong interpretation of it. They said that we had signed an agreement accepting the new constitutional and legal order of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you indeed accept the new constitutional legal order of Croatia via that agreement as the Croatian side reported?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no such provision in the Daruvar agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And by doing so, did Croatia, in fact, undermine the agreement and did it expose you to public condemnation?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that following that, there were consequences as far as you were concerned, that you were removed from office.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After you were removed and after this step by the Croatian authorities, did you continue to attempt to reach any agreement with the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In what period of time, following the Daruvar agreement?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was once I became president of Pakrac municipality, in late May of 1993. I advocated that the checkpoints should continue to exist, that people should continue to meet and to communicate. I believed that to be very important in order to normalise the relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You already spoke about that, Mr. Dzakula. Did you inform the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina of your steps and actions or did you inform any other organ?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need to inform them because these were not contacts, direct contacts, with the Croatian side. Rather, we talked with the representatives of the UN who were there in order to provide protection, and create the circumstances needed in order to have the refugees return and the situation become normalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to contacts with the UN representatives, did you have any contacts with Croatian authorities concerning that issue, and with those intentions?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said you were arrested and you spent a number of days in prison, I think you said 73 days; is that right, Mr. Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time around it was 73 days, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were arrested by the police of the Serbian Krajina, is that true?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said the investigation was led by an investigating magistrate of a Tribunal dealing with your case, is that true?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You were shown a document to extend your detention. I think you saw the document two days ago.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You must remember that document quite well. This document was extending your detention pursuant to an order of the investigating magistrate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dzakula. Just to jog our memory about something that happened in September 1993, everything that we have said about the Daruvar agreement and the events that followed, this occurred between the beginning of 1993 and now we are coming to September. In September 1993, something occurred that is usually referred to as the "Medak Pocket." Do you know anything about that, Mr. Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the Medak pocket is the area around Medak. This is in Lika just off the Velebit. This was an operation by the Croatian army and police. In the course of this operation, a significant number of civilians were killed and a considerable number of Serb villages that were under UN protection were burned. These at the time were part of territory known as the Republic of Serb -- Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I stating the names correctly when I name the following villages, Citluk, Sitovo [phoen], and Pocetelj were entirely destroyed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about a statement made by Jean Cot an UNPROFOR general who visited the area in September, the area of the Medak operation? He said, "I went to the area and I found no traces of life, human life or animal life. The destruction was systematic, deliberate and thorough." Have you heard of this statement General Cot was reputed to have made this statement. Do you remember this statement?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 29th of March 1993, the Zagreb agreement was signed? If I may be of assistance, an agreement on the cessation of hostilities signed by the Serbian side too?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the international community in fact broker the signing of this agreement? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know they mediated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a provision of this agreement saying that all the hostilities should cease and that the warring parties should be separated by moving the artillery 20 kilometres off the front line, the tanks ten kilometres, and infantry weapons one kilometre?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear about this but my memory is not very clear right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the Serb side complied with that agreement?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about Operation Flash, which occurred in May 1995. Can you tell us again about that operation, please? What was the nature of this operation?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an operation involving the military and the police. This occurred after the Zagreb-Belgrade road across Western Slavonia was closed off, in the morning hours of the 1st of May, there were breakthroughs being plead by the Croatian forces in at least two or three different places. We were cut off and entirely surrounded. We just heard that down south the area around Okucani and the surrounding villages had been evacuated. There was a lot of fighting. Many people were killed along the road to Bosanska Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, I'm sorry for interrupting you. Who were the people killed along the road to Bosanska Gradiska, were those soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both, because civilians were retreating in their cars or whatever else they had. They were fleeing across Okucani and to Bosanska Gradiska. They were being pounded by artillery weapons, the column of civilians, too, pounded by artillery and other kinds of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could one perhaps say that there were numerous casualties among the civilians who made up the column?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard some accounts from people who were part of the column and they said that there were a lot of civilians who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps share an interesting detail with us? You heard firsthand accounts from eyewitnesses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They said they were being killed from Rasnik, that they were being pounded by the air force. They said that after the massacre, the road was washed in order to conceal all the blood and any evidence of the killing that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was mediation by the UN and that you tried to have a cease-fire implemented. Is that correct, Mr. Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My colleagues and I managed to get in touch with the UN and we asked for negotiations. We asked for a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How long did the negotiations go on before you were arrested by the Croatian authorities this time around?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went on for two and a half days, nearly three days, two days. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We have to wait up for the interpreter. If the operation commenced on the 1st of May, I suppose you're talking about the 3rd of May, then.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was shelling throughout the day on the 1st of May. It was in the afternoon hours that I got in touch with the UN, the negotiations occurred on the 2nd and 3rd and, on the 4th, once the negotiations had been entering their final stage, they were postponed and the final round of shelling began at about 2 or 3 in the afternoon, and the surrender came at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I can please briefly take you back to the suffering of the columns of people who were pounded by the air force, by airplanes, did they mention the infantry fire, too, and artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is the forest of Prasina [phoen] which straddles the road to Bosanska Gradiska. They said they were -- there was gun fire from machine-guns pounding this column of civilians that was moving along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Lieutenant Colonel Harambasic ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of a brigade in Pakrac. He was part of the negotiating team, both with the UN and with the Croatian side on our behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you negotiating on behalf of his unit too?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a joint agreement that we had to hand over our weapons to UNPROFOR, which was eventually done, but then later a request came for all of us to surrender who were in the area. The civilians as well as any soldiers who had been disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say an agreement. Was this an agreement that was reached between UNPROFOR and the Serb side or were the Croats involved too?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All three sides were involved, the Croats, UNPROFOR and the Serb side, that is ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that it was agreed on the occasion that the Serbs should hand over their weapons to representatives of the UN and that they should be allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what was agreed, that the weapons should be handed over and that those who so wished would be escorted out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the numbers of soldiers involved and those of the civilians involved?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 1.500 men of military age, and a total of about 4.000 civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you not say a while ago that after the Serbs had handed over their weapons and complied with the agreement, despite the terms of the agreement, the Croats arrested them and imprisoned them?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before they were arrested, the shelling had begun. This was entirely unexpected. We requested a cease-fire. Representatives of UNPROFOR and European monitors were with us. The other side said that they would stop firing only if there was unconditional surrender. They requested our unconditional surrender immediately. And I said that I myself or anybody else should not be making a decision on behalf of all the other people. I just asked for the shelling to stop because everybody was afraid that they would be killed and that's when the surrender took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you said there was shelling. What about these people, the civilians or Serb soldiers? Where were they and who shelled them?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs were withdrawing from the villages in the fringe areas that were torn by conflict. They were in Brusnik, Kraguj, Gavanica [phoen], Seonica, Japaga, and these were also the villages that were being shelled. The entire area was being pounded by artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about the period preceding this? Did the Serbs do anything to provoke this, since you've already said that they had handed over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs had already handed over their weapons and they certainly did nothing to provoke an action like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the witness has not actually answered your question as to who was doing the shelling as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have heard the judge's question. Can you please answer, Witness?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were arrested or taken prisoner on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the early information that we received, over 500 people aged between 18 and 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to how many Serb civilians left the area of western Slavonia that was affected by Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 20.000. That was our assessment at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The UN indicated that immediately after this, a mere 800 civilians remained in the area. Would this seem to be correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to a list that we drew up immediately after Operation Flash in order to be familiar with the numbers of people still in the area, because we were afraid that some of them might be killed or might disappear, the figure that we arrived at was 1.250.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So there were about 20.000 to begin with and all those that remained the figure would be about 1.250, to understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since you drew up the list, do you know anything about what happened to the property of the people there? Do you know anything about casualties among the women and children?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were casualties in the Pakrac area. We somehow kept an eye on them but as for Okucani this was outside our reach in a manner of speaking. You couldn't go there. It wasn't safe. We heard stories about what had been going on there but we never had reliable information on how many had been killed or how many had gone missing. The reports still keep arriving. The houses in the Okucani area had been looted and a rather small number of them had been burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said something about hearing about the Croatian army washing the road, to wash away the blood, in order to conceal any evidence of their crimes. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a story that was being passed on after the war throughout Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the number of casualties? It's been ten years since. More, 11.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No reliable information. The first figure published in the media following Operation Flash, Minister Susak said about 400 people had been killed. This was never confirmed or denied, as far as I know. The figure being bandied did about now is about 100 but there is no official information. Reports on missing persons keep turning up and the number seems to be growing but I haven't been keeping track lately because there are organisations on the ground who are doing just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So the attack against this UN protected zone in Western Slavonia was over. This was on the 1st of May and onwards. Do you know what occurred on the 4th of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of August 1995, Operation Storm took place. It also lasted four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which area came under attack and was this area also a UN-protected area?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This area was also under UN protection. It was the area that formerly belonged to the SAO Krajina or the Republic of Serbian Krajina, later, from Zadar and its hinterland, and then all the way up north to Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who attacked the area and what forces were involved, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a police and military operation. I know that there were large forces involved but I'm not familiar with the exact numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this area under UN protection and were blue helmets, UN blue helmets in the area, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were artillery, the air force, tanks, and the most up-to-date weapons used during the operation?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I heard in the media, the answer seems to be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What seems to have happened to the population of the -- of sector south, as you call it, of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the population fled the area. Those who remained were subjected to mistreatment. People were killed and their property was torched or looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the indictment against the Generals, Marko Cermak and Gotovina, that exist before this Tribunal, there is talk of 22.000 houses that were burned in sector south. Are you familiar with that figure?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Serb civilians had to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, they discussed the figure of 200.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever establish and is it known how many Serbs remained and what fate befell them?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible to establish because the area is quite large. At the time, it was impossible to tour the area because it was blocked by Croatian -- it was cut off by Croatian police forces, which were present there, so we were unable to determine how many people had remained and how many had been killed. They are still looking for people and the number of the missing persons is growing, as the refugees are returning. This is the kind of information you would need to request from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the figures of the dead and missing persons?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The total number of the Serbs who were killed is 1500 -- no, I apologise. This is the number of the missing. As for the number of people who were killed, I don't know that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you are talking about those who were killed and went missing in the Operation Storm on the 4th of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I'm referring to the missing persons, I'm referring to the entire territory of Croatia. As for the victims, I don't know the total number of those who were killed. People are using such figures as 200 or 400 and I do not like to speculate when it comes to these numbers. I think it's disrespectful to the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Veritas, Mr. Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is its field of activity?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This organisation mostly investigates the number of those who were killed and went missing in the war with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the facts given by Veritas, saying that 791 [as interpreted] Serbs were killed or went missing in the Operation Storm? We are now referring to civilians. 996 civilians out of which 444 women and 11 children.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of these figures but as I told you, that figure is not constant. It keeps changing. Both when it comes to the dead and the missing. The numbers keep changing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the transcript reads 791, whereas I said 1.791. Could this be corrected, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Line 18. Line 18?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, line 17 and 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That line 17 Says, "Did you hear about the facts given by Veritas saying that 791 Serbs were killed or went missing in Operation Storm." And now it seems to me you said 791. You didn't say 1.791. And you're saying it must be corrected to 791?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I told the witness that there were 1.791 victims. However, the number recorded in the transcript is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see. 791 is wrong. It should be 1.791? Is that all you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. May the record, then, show the correction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, we mentioned the figure of 22.000 destroyed homes. Does this refer only to the houses or all facilities and outbuildings?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, entire properties were destroyed, both residential houses and all other buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that a lot of people went missing. It's been ten years since the war ended and these people are still listed as missing?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. The troops of the United Nations which arrived in this area mid-1992, to the UN safe areas, in order to protect all of the population, including the Serb population. Did they accomplish their mission?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that the expectations were not met. The protection was not implemented. Military operations were carried out which led to exodus and to a large number of persons who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you touched upon the crimes. You mentioned that there were some in 1991, 1992, 3, 4, and so on. So from 1991 onwards, were you ever an eyewitness of any crime? Did you talk directly to any of the victims of such crimes?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not an eyewitness of any murder. However, I spoke to people whose close ones were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said several times that you heard on the Croatian media reports of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned 1991, Skabrnja, Kruska, Kostajnica, and other locations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned these locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the period of time when there were renewed and intense attacks of the Croatian forces against barracks, soldiers, and the population, that was in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just an objection to that last question. That question, I would suggest, is several different questions rolled into one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milovancevic, I think you've got quite a number of questions there. I think you can break them up. It's not clear what the yes refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I understood Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you spoke today about how the barracks were surrounded and seized throughout Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the barracks of the federal armed forces were not only attacked by means of weapons, surrounded, seized, but that they were also subjected to severe, hostile propaganda of Croatian media?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were the federal armed forces referred to as Serb Chetnik occupation army or forces?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA forces step out of their state territory by an inch?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned how the JNA forces and members of the Territorial Defence were killed mercilessly. You mentioned one location, the bridge in -- on the Korana river; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say to the Prosecutor that you heard on the Croatian media that Yugoslav communist, Serb, Chetnik army was attacking Croatian villages and seizing them?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, or rather occupying them [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear or read in the press that there were any Croatian forces of the formation of company and higher deployed there?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have such direct information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you heard about this from the press.

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the press report that there were regular clashes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt? I here you, Mr. Milovancevic, talking simultaneously with the interpreter. She's desperately trying to keep pace with you. Could you please slow down. Otherwise you're talking both at the same time and I doubt that she is managing to keep pace with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a favour to ask. If I'm going too fast, the interpreters should warn me. Sometimes I simply neglect the fact or I lose myself in the questions that I'm putting and I don't do this wishing to create problems. On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can I -- Your Honour, if I could just make a suggestion. From my experience with the interpreters, not only do they like us to slow down but also in this circumstance where they are speaking the same language they actually ask that each party, the lawyer and the witness, insert a pause at the end of the question, so that when the question is finished, the witness should pause for a moment before answering and the same when the answer is finished, there should be a pause. The interpreters are very aided if those pauses are inserted, in addition to slowing down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic, I'm afraid we are not supposed to be losing ourselves during the trial. We can lose ourselves anywhere else but here. So I will ask you to please remember that you are not just having a communication with the witness out anywhere else. You are in court. You've got to be recorded. You've got to be interpreted. Everybody must keep pace with you, even the stenographers must keep pace with you. I've heard the request that there must be a pause. When you hear yourself speaking at the same time as the interpreter, that should be a warning to you that you're talking too fast. Please slow down. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you heard from the Croatian media about the attacks against Croatian villages carried out by the federal forces, the JNA together with the Territorial Defence, and that Croatian civilians were killed in those operations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Croatian media reported on these cases depicting them as clashes that their forces had with the federal forces?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they reported on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When speaking about the situation on the ground, did you ever say that radio and telephone lines in Croatia, especially in Slavonia, were disrupted and that there were electricity blackouts, particularly from August 1992 onwards?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you said that due to the electricity shortages, it was impossible to watch television, to listen to the other media outlets, and that only those who had radio stations such as police and members of the TO could follow the media and that there were very few such cases?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only people who had battery-operated radios could follow these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I quoting your words correctly when I say that in the beginning of your evidence, you said that the Croatian media reported on the events in one way and that the remaining media, the Serbian media, reported on the events in a different way?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, did Croatia wage an enormous propaganda war against its own state, Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information indicating that the Croatian side exaggerated on the number of the victims and on the events themselves?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you said that for a long time, you've been working in the Serbian Democratic Forum; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's been 11 years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that the Serbian Democratic Forum was founded in June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Prosecution put a letter to you signed by Mrs. Ljubisa Solaja, president of the Serbian democratic party of the Krajina, pertaining to your activities?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But not to my activities. Rather, to the founding of the Serbian Democratic Forum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please show the following Prosecution exhibit on the screen, that is Prosecution Exhibit number 1. Your Honours, if this letter is not in the system, then perhaps we could have it placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read the title to us?

utterances.speaker: VELIJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "An announcement of the Serbian Democratic Party of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
